questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 9 days after returning from a trip to Nigeria, where she did not take prophylaxis. She has had daily fevers for 4 days and today became confused and had a seizure. Temperature is 40.1 C (104.2 F). A thin smear shows 12% of red blood cells infected, many with two or more small ring forms, some rings sitting at the edge of the cell, and a few crescent-shaped gametocytes.

Which of the following best explains her neurologic findings?
choices: Immune complex deposition within small cerebral vessel walls
Direct invasion of neurons by sporozoites
Infected red cells adhering to capillary endothelium

explain.html: P. falciparum is the species that kills, and its virulence comes from what it does to the red cell surface. It places PfEMP1 on infected red cells, which permits cytoadherence: infected cells stick to the endothelium of peripheral capillaries and sludge, blocking blood flow. Falciparum also invades red cells of every age and lets several merozoites enter one cell, so it multiplies fast and parasitemia climbs. When the sludging happens in the brain, the result is cerebral malaria, with abnormal behavior, confusion, obtundation and seizures. In this patient, 12% parasitemia, multiple rings per cell, applique forms at the cell edge and banana-shaped gametocytes identify falciparum, and her confusion and seizure come from microvascular obstruction. Untreated falciparum is fatal, so this picture is an emergency.
why: Falciparum forms no hypnozoites; liver dormancy belongs to P. vivax and P. ovale.
Cerebral malaria comes from infected red cells adhering to and blocking cerebral capillaries, not from immune complex deposits.
Hemoglobinuria (blackwater fever) injures the kidney, not the brain.
Sporozoites travel from the bite to liver cells, not into neurons.
explain.takeaway: P. falciparum PfEMP1 makes infected red cells adhere to capillary endothelium, causing microvascular obstruction and cerebral malaria.
explain.topic: P. falciparum virulence and cerebral malaria
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: Falciparum forms no hypnozoites; liver dormancy belongs to P. vivax and P. ovale.
rows.if_right: a relapse months after travel with Schuffner dots on the smear

rows.why: Cerebral malaria comes from infected red cells adhering to and blocking cerebral capillaries, not from immune complex deposits.
rows.if_right: renal involvement, such as nephrotic syndrome in a patient with P. malariae

rows.why: Hemoglobinuria (blackwater fever) injures the kidney, not the brain.
rows.if_right: dark urine and acute renal failure rather than confusion and seizure

rows.if_right: a mosquito bite delivering the stage that travels through blood to hepatocytes

questions.stem:
A 40-year-old man returning from Ghana has fever, chills and myalgias. The laboratory prepares two Giemsa-stained preparations from the same blood sample. In the first, the red cells have been lysed and parasites are seen scattered between white cells. In the second, intact red cells are spread in a single layer.

What is the second preparation used for that the first cannot provide?
choices: Detecting low-level parasitemia with higher sensitivity
Confirming that hypnozoites are present in the liver
Detecting parasite antigen without a microscope
Identifying the species and the percent of infected cells
Measuring antibody titers against the parasite

explain.html: Light microscopy of a Giemsa-stained blood smear is the gold standard for malaria, and the two smear types answer different questions. The thick smear lyses red cells and concentrates the blood, so parasites lie outside cells and are easier to find, giving higher sensitivity for detection. The thin smear keeps red cells intact in a single layer, so the position of the parasite in the cell, the cell's size and features like Schuffner dots or band forms can be seen. That makes the thin smear the tool to determine the species and the degree of parasitemia. In this vignette the first preparation, with lysed cells, is the thick smear and the second is the thin smear. Because parasitemia can lag behind symptoms, smears can be repeated every 12 hours for three sets before malaria is excluded.
explain.table:
TestHow it worksWhat it tells you
Thick smearRed cells lysed, blood concentratedWhether parasites are present (more sensitive)
Thin smearIntact red cells in one layerSpecies and percent parasitemia
Rapid diagnostic testImmunochromatography on a finger prickParasite antigen without a microscope
why: Higher sensitivity for finding parasites is the strength of the thick smear, the first preparation.
Hypnozoites live in hepatocytes and never appear on a blood smear.
Antigen detection without a microscope is the rapid diagnostic test.
Smears show the parasite itself, and malaria is diagnosed by smear rather than antibody titers.
explain.takeaway: Thick smears detect malaria parasites with higher sensitivity, while thin smears identify the Plasmodium species and quantify parasitemia.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: Higher sensitivity for finding parasites is the strength of the thick smear, the first preparation.

rows.if_right: a liver sample, which is not part of malaria diagnosis

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman who emigrated from a tropical region several years ago reports fevers that come every fourth day (fever on day 1, then again on day 4, then day 7). Between episodes she feels well. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein, and she has new ankle edema. A thin smear shows trophozoites stretched across the red cell as a band and schizonts arranged as a rosette.

Which feature of this organism best accounts for her illness arising years after exposure?
choices: Persistent low-level parasites in red blood cells
Dormant hepatic hypnozoites that later mature into merozoites
Rapid multiplication in red cells of all ages
Cytoadherence of infected cells in glomeruli

explain.html: The fever pattern in malaria reflects how often schizonts rupture, and each species has its own rhythm. P. vivax and P. ovale give tertian fevers (rupture every 36 to 48 hours), falciparum gives irregular or daily fevers, and P. malariae gives quartan fevers with rupture every 72 hours. P. malariae is the least pathogenic species, has the longest incubation and shows band-form trophozoites and rosette schizonts on thin smear. Its classic complication is nephrotic syndrome, which explains her proteinuria and ankle edema. It has no liver dormancy; instead it persists at low levels in red blood cells, and symptoms return from that blood reservoir years later, which is called recrudescence. This is the key distinction from vivax and ovale, which relapse from hypnozoites.
explain.table:
SpeciesFever patternSmear clueHow late illness returns
P. malariaeQuartan (every 72 hours)Band forms, rosette schizontsRecrudescence from persistent blood parasites
P. vivax / P. ovaleTertian (36 to 48 hours)Schuffner dotsRelapse from liver hypnozoites
P. falciparumQuotidian (daily)Multiple rings, applique, crescent gametocytesDoes not persist; acute, severe
why: Hypnozoites belong to P. vivax and P. ovale, which show Schuffner dots, not band forms.
Selective invasion of young red cells describes P. vivax.
Invading red cells of all ages and multiplying fast describes P. falciparum.
Cytoadherence is the falciparum PfEMP1 mechanism and is not how P. malariae injures the kidney.
explain.takeaway: P. malariae causes quartan fevers, band-form trophozoites and nephrotic syndrome, and recurs years later by recrudescence from persistent blood-stage parasites.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: Hypnozoites belong to P. vivax and P. ovale, which show Schuffner dots, not band forms.
rows.if_right: tertian fevers and Schuffner dots in enlarged red cells

rows.why: Selective invasion of young red cells describes P. vivax.
rows.if_right: a Duffy-dependent species infecting only immature red cells

rows.why: Invading red cells of all ages and multiplying fast describes P. falciparum.
rows.if_right: high parasitemia with multiple rings per cell and severe anemia

rows.why: Cytoadherence is the falciparum PfEMP1 mechanism and is not how P. malariae injures the kidney.
rows.if_right: cerebral malaria with applique rings and crescent gametocytes

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old man develops fever, headache and myalgias 12 days after returning from Kenya. He is alert, eating and drinking, and has normal blood pressure and glucose. A thin smear shows ring forms in 1% of red cells with occasional crescent-shaped gametocytes. The region he visited has widespread chloroquine resistance.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

explain.html: Malaria treatment depends on two questions: was the infection acquired where chloroquine still works, and is the disease uncomplicated or severe. Chloroquine treats only sensitive infections, which for falciparum means a few regions such as Haiti and the Dominican Republic. In chloroquine-resistant areas the first line is artemisinin-based therapy, the most active antimalarials, which clear early ring forms quickly and reduce gametocyte carriage. Uncomplicated disease gets oral artemether-lumefantrine, with atovaquone-proguanil as the alternative, while severe malaria gets IV artesunate. This man has falciparum (crescent gametocytes) from Kenya, 1% parasitemia, normal mental status, blood pressure and glucose, so he has uncomplicated resistant malaria. Reserving IV artesunate for severe disease, such as hyperparasitemia over 5%, cerebral malaria or organ failure, keeps treatment matched to risk.
explain.table:
SituationTreatment
Chloroquine-sensitive (P. malariae, sensitive falciparum)Chloroquine
P. vivax or P. ovaleChloroquine, then primaquine or tafenoquine
Chloroquine-resistant, uncomplicatedArtemether-lumefantrine or atovaquone-proguanil
Severe malariaIV artesunate
why: Chloroquine fails in resistant falciparum, and primaquine targets vivax and ovale liver forms that falciparum lacks.
IV artesunate is reserved for severe malaria, and he has none of its features.
Benznidazole treats Chagas disease, not malaria.
Doxycycline is a malaria prophylaxis drug, not single-drug treatment of acute falciparum malaria.
explain.takeaway: Uncomplicated chloroquine-resistant malaria is treated with artemether-lumefantrine or atovaquone-proguanil, while severe malaria requires IV artesunate.
explain.topic: Malaria treatment by resistance and severity
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.if_right: P. vivax acquired in a chloroquine-sensitive area

questions.stem:
A research group engineers a mosquito strain that cannot be infected when it feeds on a person with malaria. Mosquitoes of the normal strain become infected when they feed on the same person. The defect blocks the parasite at the first step of its development inside the mosquito.

Which parasite stage, taken up from human blood, is the engineered mosquito unable to support?

explain.html: The Plasmodium life cycle moves between mosquito and human, and each handoff uses a specific stage. The female Anopheles mosquito injects sporozoites, which travel in the blood to liver cells, replicate as schizonts and release merozoites when the liver cells rupture. Merozoites infect red cells and become ring-form (immature) trophozoites, then mature trophozoites and schizonts that rupture to infect more red cells. Some ring forms instead differentiate into the sexual stage, the gametocytes. Gametocytes are the stage ingested by the mosquito when it feeds, so they are the first stage the parasite needs inside the mosquito. A mosquito that cannot support gametocytes therefore cannot become infected, which is also why artemisinins, by reducing gametocyte carriage, help limit transmission.
explain.table:
StageWhere it is
SporozoiteInjected by the mosquito, travels to liver
Schizont (liver)Replicates in hepatocytes
MerozoiteReleased from liver or red cells, infects red cells
Ring-form trophozoiteEarly stage inside red cells
GametocyteSexual stage in blood, ingested by the mosquito
why: Sporozoites are what the mosquito injects, not what it takes up.
Merozoites infect human red cells and do not continue the cycle in the mosquito.
Ring forms are the early stage inside human red cells, not the stage the mosquito uses.
Liver schizonts sit in hepatocytes and are not in the blood meal.
explain.takeaway: Gametocytes, the sexual blood stage of Plasmodium, are ingested by the Anopheles mosquito, while sporozoites are the stage it injects.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: Sporozoites are what the mosquito injects, not what it takes up.

rows.why: Merozoites infect human red cells and do not continue the cycle in the mosquito.
rows.if_right: a block of the stage released from ruptured liver schizonts to invade red cells

rows.why: Ring forms are the early stage inside human red cells, not the stage the mosquito uses.
rows.if_right: a block of the earliest red cell stage, seen as rings on a thin smear

rows.if_right: a drug acting on the stage that replicates in hepatocytes after the bite

questions.stem:
A 71-year-old man with diabetes and chronic kidney disease in New Jersey is admitted in late August with 3 days of fever and headache followed by confusion and weakness of the left arm with absent reflexes. He has been gardening in the evenings and has many mosquito bites. He has not traveled. Cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with mildly elevated protein and normal glucose.

Which of the following tests is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Thin blood smear for intracellular parasites
IgM antibody against the virus in serum and cerebrospinal fluid
Card agglutination test followed by lymph node aspiration
Wright-stained peripheral blood smear examined for intracellular morulae
Western blot for IgM and IgG bands

explain.html: Arboviral encephalitis is brain inflammation from an insect-borne virus, and West Nile virus is the leading cause in the US. It is carried by the Culex mosquito, peaks in summer and early fall, and treats humans and horses as dead-end hosts. About 80% of infections are asymptomatic, about 20% cause West Nile fever, and fewer than 1% become neuroinvasive disease, with risk concentrated in people over 60 and those with cancer, diabetes, kidney disease or transplant. Neuroinvasive disease brings fever, headache, altered mental status, seizure and acute flaccid paralysis, and some deficits are permanent. This 71-year-old with diabetes and kidney disease, evening mosquito exposure in late August, encephalitis and a flaccid arm fits exactly. The diagnosis is made with West Nile IgM in serum and CSF, and treatment is supportive care.
why: A thin smear looks for intracellular parasites such as Plasmodium or Babesia, not a virus.
The card agglutination test with lymph node aspiration diagnoses African trypanosomiasis.
Morulae on a Wright stain point to Anaplasma or Ehrlichia.
Western blot banding confirms a positive Lyme antibody screen.
explain.takeaway: West Nile neuroinvasive disease, spread by Culex mosquitoes and striking elderly or comorbid patients in late summer, is diagnosed by IgM in serum and CSF and treated supportively.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: A thin smear looks for intracellular parasites such as Plasmodium or Babesia, not a virus.
rows.if_right: a returning traveler or tick-exposed patient with fever and hemolytic anemia

rows.why: The card agglutination test with lymph node aspiration diagnoses African trypanosomiasis.
rows.if_right: a traveler to Africa with a tsetse fly chancre and sleepiness

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man returns from a trip to rural Brazil and develops fever, myalgias and vomiting that improve after 2 days. On the third day the fever returns with jaundice, bleeding gums and decreased urine output. Laboratory studies show markedly elevated aminotransferases, a prolonged prothrombin time and rising creatinine. He did not receive any travel vaccines.

Which of the following would most likely have prevented this illness?
choices: A live, attenuated viral vaccine before travel
Doxycycline taken after any insect bite
Boiling water and avoiding raw food

explain.html: Yellow fever is a mosquito-borne viral hemorrhagic fever caused by a single-stranded RNA flavivirus and carried by the Aedes mosquito. It is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa and equatorial South America, with a recent epidemic in Brazil. The illness ranges from asymptomatic to a self-limited febrile illness to life-threatening hemorrhagic fever. The typical course is fever, malaise, pain and vomiting that remit after about 2 days; if fever returns on day 3, it can bring hepatic injury, renal failure and coagulopathy, and late shock. This traveler to rural Brazil follows that biphasic course with jaundice, bleeding and rising creatinine. Yellow fever is prevented with a live, attenuated vaccine, so the missed travel vaccine is what would have changed the outcome.
why: Atovaquone-proguanil is malaria prophylaxis and does nothing against a flavivirus.
Doxycycline targets bacteria such as rickettsiae, not a virus.
Anopheles, the nighttime biter, transmits malaria; yellow fever is spread by Aedes.
Yellow fever is mosquito-borne, not food or water-borne.
explain.takeaway: Yellow fever, an Aedes-borne flavivirus, causes hepatic injury, coagulopathy and renal failure after a brief remission and is prevented by a live, attenuated vaccine.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: Atovaquone-proguanil is malaria prophylaxis and does nothing against a flavivirus.
rows.if_right: a traveler wanting protection against malaria in an endemic area

rows.why: Doxycycline targets bacteria such as rickettsiae, not a virus.
rows.if_right: a tick-borne rickettsial infection such as RMSF

rows.why: Anopheles, the nighttime biter, transmits malaria; yellow fever is spread by Aedes.
rows.if_right: prevention of malaria rather than an Aedes-borne virus

questions.stem:
A 16-year-old boy in North Carolina is brought to the clinic in June with 4 days of fever to 39.8 C (103.6 F), severe headache and myalgias. Two days after the fever began, flat pink spots appeared on his wrists and ankles; they have since spread to the trunk and now include the palms and soles, and some lesions look petechial. His face is spared. He walked through tall grass with his dog last week.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
choices: Wait for paired serology before treating

explain.html: Rickettsiae are divided into the spotted fever group and the typhus group, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii) is the most common rickettsial disease in the US. It is carried by Dermacentor (dog) ticks and the Lone Star tick from May to September, with an incubation of about 7 days. It starts with high fever and headache, and after about 3 days roughly 90% develop a macular rash that begins on the wrists and ankles, spreads inward to the trunk, can involve the palms and soles and spares the face. A spotted or petechial rash around day 5 or 6 signals more severe disease, which can progress to multiorgan failure and shock. This boy's June tick-season exposure and centripetal, petechial rash fit RMSF. Because it can kill within days, the diagnosis is clinical and doxycycline is started immediately rather than waiting for antibody or PCR results.
why: The diagnosis is clinical, and delaying treatment for serology risks death within days.
Chloroquine is an antimalarial and does not treat rickettsiae.
Amoxicillin is an early Lyme disease option and does not treat rickettsiae.
RMSF has a high mortality without antibiotics, so supportive care alone is wrong.
explain.takeaway: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (tick exposure, rash spreading from wrists and ankles to the trunk including palms and soles) is diagnosed clinically and treated with doxycycline immediately.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.if_right: a traveler with malaria acquired in a chloroquine-sensitive area

questions.stem:
A 60-year-old man in Connecticut presents in July with 5 days of fever, headache and myalgias. He has no rash. He removed a small tick from his leg 10 days ago. A peripheral blood smear with Wright stain shows intracytoplasmic clusters of bacteria inside neutrophils.

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the most likely vector of this organism?

explain.html: Anaplasma and Ehrlichia are obligate intracellular rickettsiae in the family Anaplasmataceae, and they are told apart by the cell they infect and the tick that carries them. Anaplasma phagocytophilum causes human granulocytic anaplasmosis, forms morulae in granulocytes and is carried by Ixodes scapularis (deer tick) in the Northeast and Midwest. Ehrlichia chaffeensis causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis, forms morulae in monocytes and is carried by the Lone Star tick in the Southeast and mid-Atlantic. Both cause fever, headache and myalgias with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and elevated liver enzymes; rash and CNS involvement are rare in anaplasmosis. This Connecticut patient with a tick bite, no rash, those labs and morulae inside neutrophils has anaplasmosis, so the vector is the deer tick. Both infections are treated with doxycycline.
explain.table:
FeatureAnaplasmosisEhrlichiosis
Cell infectedGranulocyteMonocyte
VectorIxodes scapularis (deer tick)Amblyomma (Lone Star tick)
GeographyNortheast, MidwestSoutheast, mid-Atlantic, Midwest
RashRareAbout one third
LabsLeukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated liver enzymesSame
TreatmentDoxycyclineDoxycycline
why: The Lone Star tick carries Ehrlichia, whose morulae sit in monocytes.
The Dermacentor tick is the main vector of RMSF, which causes a centripetal rash.
Triatomine bugs transmit Trypanosoma cruzi.
Aedes mosquitoes carry yellow fever, dengue, Zika and chikungunya, not rickettsiae.
explain.takeaway: Anaplasma phagocytophilum forms morulae in granulocytes and is carried by Ixodes scapularis, whereas Ehrlichia forms morulae in monocytes and is carried by the Lone Star tick; both cause leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis and respond to doxycycline.

rows.if_right: morulae inside monocytes in a patient from the Southeast

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man in Maine presents in June with 4 days of fatigue and low-grade fever. On his calf there is an 8-cm painless, nonpruritic red patch with central clearing that has enlarged over several days. He recalls pulling off a small tick about 2 weeks ago. He has no joint, cardiac or neurologic findings.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Order serum Lyme antibody before deciding on treatment
Order a Western blot for IgM and IgG bands
Treat with doxycycline without laboratory testing
Perform a skin biopsy for PCR
Order a peripheral smear for morulae

explain.html: Lyme disease is transmitted by the Ixodes deer tick, which must be attached for 36 to 48 hours, and its first stage is early localized disease 3 to 30 days after the bite. About 70% of patients develop erythema migrans, a painless, nonpruritic expanding lesion that can look like the classic bulls-eye or a variation of it. The diagnostic algorithm starts with one question: is erythema migrans present? If it is, the diagnosis is made clinically and no lab tests are needed. If it is not, serum Lyme antibody is checked, and a positive screen is confirmed by Western blot (2 IgM bands or 5 IgG bands). This man has an expanding 8-cm painless lesion with central clearing two weeks after a tick bite, so he has erythema migrans and should simply be treated with doxycycline, which also covers anaplasmosis and ehrlichiosis.
why: Antibody testing is the path only when erythema migrans is absent.
Western blot confirms a positive antibody screen and is not needed when erythema migrans is present.
PCR on a skin biopsy is the adjunct test listed for RMSF, not Lyme disease.
Morulae are sought for Anaplasma or Ehrlichia.
explain.takeaway: Erythema migrans establishes the diagnosis of early Lyme disease clinically, so treatment starts without lab testing; antibody screening with Western blot confirmation is reserved for patients without the rash.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.why: PCR on a skin biopsy is the adjunct test listed for RMSF, not Lyme disease.

questions.stem:
A 37-year-old wildlife photographer returns from 3 weeks on the savannah of Tanzania. A painful swelling appeared at the site of a fly bite on his arm during the trip. Over the last 2 weeks he has had intermittent fevers and headaches, and now he is confused and somnolent. A card agglutination test is positive and lymph node aspirate shows trypomastigotes.

Which of the following best describes this infection compared with the West African form?
choices: Chronic course over years with humans as the main host
Dormant liver stage causing relapse years later
Spread by triatomine bugs living in house walls
Transmitted by sandflies, causing skin ulcers
Acute course with central nervous system disease within weeks

explain.html: African sleeping sickness is caused by Trypanosoma brucei, spread by the tsetse fly, and its two subspecies run very different courses. The bite leaves a painful chancre, trypomastigotes enter the bloodstream and early symptoms are intermittent headache, fever, malaise and arthralgias. T. b. rhodesiense in the dry savannah of East Africa has animals as its primary host and causes acute epidemic disease, with meningoencephalitis within weeks and death within months. T. b. gambiense in humid Central and West Africa has humans as the primary host and progresses slowly over about three years with personality change, sleepiness and confusion. This photographer from the Tanzanian savannah with a chancre and confusion within weeks has the East African form. Diagnosis is a card agglutination test followed by lymphatic aspiration, and early rhodesiense is treated with suramin, late with melarsoprol.
explain.table:
FeatureT. b. rhodesienseT. b. gambiense
RegionEast Africa, dry savannahCentral and West Africa, humid areas
Primary hostAnimalsHumans
CourseAcute, CNS within weeks, death within monthsChronic, about 3 years
Early treatmentSuraminPentamidine
Late treatmentMelarsoprolNifurtimox-eflornithine
why: A slow course over years with humans as the host describes T. b. gambiense.
Liver dormancy is a feature of P. vivax and P. ovale, not trypanosomes.
Triatomine bugs transmit T. cruzi, not T. brucei.
Sandflies transmit leishmaniasis, not sleeping sickness.
explain.takeaway: T. brucei rhodesiense (East Africa, animal reservoir) causes acute sleeping sickness with CNS disease within weeks, whereas T. brucei gambiense (West and Central Africa, human host) is chronic over years.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.if_right: a traveler to humid Central or West Africa with gradual sleepiness over years

rows.why: Liver dormancy is a feature of P. vivax and P. ovale, not trypanosomes.
rows.if_right: relapsing fevers months after travel with Schuffner dots on smear

rows.why: Triatomine bugs transmit T. cruzi, not T. brucei.

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old man comes to the clinic with 2 days of fever, chills, and sweats. Seven months ago he spent 6 weeks working in rural India and was treated there for a febrile illness that cleared on chloroquine alone. He has had no travel since. Temperature is 39.4 C (103 F) and the spleen tip is palpable. A thin blood smear shows enlarged red blood cells containing trophozoites with fine stippling (Schuffner dots). He is treated again with chloroquine.

Which of the following should be checked before he starts the second drug that will prevent another recurrence?

explain.html: Malaria species differ in whether they keep a persistent liver stage. P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant liver forms called hypnozoites, which can stay quiet for months to years and then mature into merozoites that seed the blood again. Chloroquine acts only on the erythrocytic stage, so it clears the red cells but leaves the liver reservoir untouched. That is why chloroquine is followed by primaquine or tafenoquine, the drugs that treat the liver stage. Here, fever returning seven months after a chloroquine-only course, enlarged red cells and Schuffner dots identify P. vivax (or P. ovale) relapsing from hypnozoites. Both liver-stage drugs carry a warning to check for G6PD deficiency first, so red cell G6PD activity is the test to send before the second drug.

A QT check does not decide whether primaquine or tafenoquine is safe; G6PD activity does.

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old woman in an apartment in New York City has 4 days of fever, chills, severe headache and photophobia. Ten days ago she noticed a painless papule on her thigh that ulcerated and is now a black crusted lesion. Today a rash of scattered papules and vesicles has appeared on her face, trunk and legs, sparing the palms and soles. She has seen mice in the building's basement. She has had no outdoor travel.

Which arthropod most likely transmitted her infection?

explain.html: The important rickettsiae are grouped by disease, and each has its own vector. In the spotted fever group, R. rickettsii (RMSF) is carried by ticks and R. akari (rickettsialpox) by mites; in the typhus group, R. prowazekii is carried by the body louse and R. typhi by fleas. Rickettsialpox has rodents as its host, which gives it an urban distribution such as New York City. Its course is biphasic: about a week after the bite a papule ulcerates into an eschar, then systemic spread brings high fever, severe headache, myalgias and photophobia, followed by a papulovesicular rash that crusts. This woman in a New York apartment with mice, an eschar and a later vesicular rash sparing the palms and soles fits rickettsialpox. It is treated with doxycycline, like the other rickettsial infections.
explain.table:
OrganismDiseaseVector
R. rickettsiiRocky Mountain spotted feverTick
R. akariRickettsialpoxMite (rodent host)
R. prowazekiiEpidemic typhusBody louse
R. typhiEndemic typhusFlea
why: The Dermacentor tick transmits RMSF, which has no eschar and does involve the palms and soles.
The body louse transmits R. prowazekii, epidemic typhus.
Culex mosquitoes transmit West Nile virus, not a rickettsia.
Fleas transmit R. typhi (endemic typhus) and plague, not R. akari.
explain.takeaway: Rickettsialpox (R. akari) is an urban, mite-borne infection from rodents that causes an eschar followed by a papulovesicular rash and is treated with doxycycline.

questions.stem:
A 22-year-old woman in Pennsylvania presents in August with lightheadedness and fatigue. Six weeks ago she had an expanding, painless, nonpruritic red patch on her thigh that faded on its own. She now has several new large ring-shaped patches on her trunk and a right facial droop. Heart rate is 42/min, and the electrocardiogram shows third-degree atrioventricular block.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

explain.html: Lyme disease, caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi and spread by Ixodes scapularis, moves through three stages. Stage 1, early localized disease, appears 3 to 30 days after the bite with erythema migrans. Stage 2, early disseminated disease, follows weeks to months later as the organism spreads in the blood, causing Bell palsy, meningitis, carditis with AV block and migratory arthritis. Stage 3 brings intermittent or persistent large-joint arthritis months to years later. This woman's faded erythema migrans, new multiple ring lesions, facial droop and third-degree heart block put her in stage 2 with carditis. Early disease and arthritis are treated with oral doxycycline, amoxicillin or cefuroxime, but high-degree heart block and persistent arthritis call for IV ceftriaxone.
explain.table:
Lyme presentationTreatment
Early localized (erythema migrans)Oral doxycycline, amoxicillin or cefuroxime
Lyme arthritisOral doxycycline, amoxicillin or cefuroxime
High-degree heart blockIV ceftriaxone
Persistent arthritisIV ceftriaxone
why: Oral amoxicillin treats early Lyme disease, not complete heart block.
Oral doxycycline is for early Lyme disease without high-degree heart block.
Oral cefuroxime is another early-disease option, not therapy for carditis.
Atovaquone plus azithromycin treats babesiosis, not a spirochete.
explain.takeaway: Lyme carditis with high-degree AV block is treated with IV ceftriaxone, while early localized Lyme disease and Lyme arthritis are treated with oral doxycycline, amoxicillin or cefuroxime.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old woman on Nantucket Island presents in July with a week of fever, chills, weakness and dark urine. She had a splenectomy after a car crash 10 years ago. She does yard work and often finds ticks on her dog. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL (12 to 16), platelets are 64,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), and aminotransferases are elevated. A thin smear shows small intraerythrocytic ring forms and a few groups of four organisms in a cross shape.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

explain.html: Babesia microti is an intra-erythrocytic protozoan transmitted by Ixodes ticks, the same vector as Lyme disease and anaplasmosis. It causes malaise, fever, chills, weakness and headache with anemia, elevated liver enzymes and thrombocytopenia. Risk factors for severe disease are history of splenectomy, HIV and TNF inhibitors. Diagnosis is by peripheral blood smear, antibody or PCR, and the smear shows ring forms and the diagnostic tetrad, or Maltese cross, inside red cells. This woman with a prior splenectomy, tick exposure, hemolysis and cross-shaped groups of four in red cells has babesiosis. Treatment is atovaquone and azithromycin; the ring forms can resemble malaria, but the tetrad and absence of travel point to Babesia.
why: Chloroquine and primaquine treat malaria, which the tetrad and lack of travel argue against.
Doxycycline treats Lyme disease, anaplasmosis and ehrlichiosis, not a red cell protozoan.
IV ceftriaxone is for Lyme carditis or persistent Lyme arthritis.
Benznidazole is used for Chagas disease.
explain.takeaway: Babesia microti, an Ixodes-borne red cell protozoan that is most severe after splenectomy, shows ring forms and Maltese cross tetrads on smear and is treated with atovaquone and azithromycin.

questions.stem:
A 49-year-old man who grew up in a rural Bolivian village in a house with a thatched roof is evaluated for progressive dyspnea, ankle swelling and palpitations. An echocardiogram shows a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle, and Holter monitoring shows intermittent heart block. He also reports years of difficulty swallowing and chronic constipation. Two different serologic tests are positive.

How was this infection most likely acquired?
choices: Bite of a female Anopheles mosquito at night
Contamination of a skin break with insect feces
Bite of a tsetse fly with a painful chancre
Inhalation of spores from contaminated soil
An Ixodes tick attached for at least 48 hours

explain.html: Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease, which is endemic in Latin America and linked to poverty and thatched-roof housing. Its vector, the triatomine bug, bites and then defecates; the person scratches, and feces containing trypomastigotes are inoculated through the break in the skin. The acute infection is usually asymptomatic or a febrile illness. Decades later the chronic phase brings cardiomyopathy, heart failure, heart block, megaesophagus and megacolon, and sudden cardiac death is the most feared outcome. This man's childhood in a rural Bolivian thatched-roof home, dilated cardiomyopathy with heart block, dysphagia, constipation and two positive serologic tests fit chronic Chagas disease. Treatment is benznidazole or nifurtimox.
why: Anopheles transmits malaria, which does not cause cardiomyopathy and megacolon decades later.
Tsetse flies transmit African trypanosomiasis, which affects the CNS, not the heart and gut decades later.
Trypanosoma cruzi enters through a skin break contaminated by triatomine bug feces and is not inhaled.
Prolonged Ixodes attachment transmits Lyme disease.
explain.takeaway: Trypanosoma cruzi enters through skin breaks contaminated by triatomine bug feces and decades later causes cardiomyopathy, heart block, megaesophagus and megacolon.

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman in Massachusetts comes to clinic in June with 3 days of fever and myalgias and a 9-cm painless, nonpruritic red patch with central clearing on her thigh. She gardens and walks in the woods near her home. She is told the rash alone makes the diagnosis and is started on oral amoxicillin. Ten days later the patch has faded, but she still has fevers to 39.0 C (102.2 F), headache, and malaise. Her urine is a normal color.

[[labs 0]]

Which change to her initial treatment would most likely have prevented this persistent illness?
choices: Adding atovaquone and azithromycin to amoxicillin
A Western blot before starting any antibiotic
Intravenous ceftriaxone in place of amoxicillin

explain.html:
Several vector-borne infections share one tick: Ixodes scapularis transmits Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease), Anaplasma phagocytophilum (human granulocytic anaplasmosis), and Babesia microti (babesiosis). Early localized Lyme disease is diagnosed clinically when erythema migrans is present and can be treated with doxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime. Anaplasmosis is an obligate intracellular infection of granulocytes that causes fever, myalgias and headache with leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and raised liver enzymes, and its treatment is doxycycline. Babesiosis also causes anemia, thrombocytopenia and liver enzyme rise, but the smear shows rings and tetrads inside red cells.

This woman was correctly diagnosed with Lyme disease from the rash and treated with amoxicillin, which cleared the patch but not her fever. Her new leukopenia, three serial smears with no intraerythrocytic organisms, and a normal bilirubin (no hemolysis) point to anaplasmosis, not babesiosis. Doxycycline also treats anaplasmosis and ehrlichiosis, so choosing it for the early Lyme disease would have covered the coinfection from the same bite.
explain.table:
Ixodes-borne infectionKey labs or smearTreatment
Lyme disease (early)Clinical diagnosis with erythema migransDoxycycline, amoxicillin, or cefuroxime
AnaplasmosisLeukopenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, high liver enzymes; morulae in granulocytesDoxycycline
BabesiosisAnemia, thrombocytopenia, high liver enzymes; rings and tetrads inside red cellsAtovaquone and azithromycin
why: Three serial smears show no intraerythrocytic rings or tetrads and bilirubin is normal, so there is no evidence of the red-cell infection that defines babesiosis.
Cefuroxime is an acceptable early Lyme drug, but it does not treat anaplasmosis, so the same gap would remain.
Erythema migrans makes the diagnosis without labs, and confirming Lyme would not have added coverage for anaplasmosis.
Intravenous ceftriaxone is reserved for high-degree heart block or persistent arthritis and does not treat anaplasmosis.
explain.takeaway: Ixodes scapularis transmits Lyme disease, anaplasmosis and babesiosis; doxycycline treats early Lyme disease and anaplasmosis together, while babesiosis needs atovaquone plus azithromycin.

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old woman develops daily fevers, chills, and myalgias 10 days after returning from 3 weeks of volunteer work in rural Ghana. Eight months ago, after a trip to the same region, she had a similar fever that resolved with a treatment she cannot name. Temperature is 39.3 C (102.7 F), blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, and glucose 92 mg/dL (70 to 100); she is alert and eating. A thin smear shows 2% parasitemia, red cells of all sizes containing small rings, several cells with two or more rings, some rings at the cell edge, and a few crescent-shaped gametocytes. Anopheles mosquitoes are active in her home community, and the health department asks about onward spread.

Which property of the most appropriate treatment most directly lowers the chance that a mosquito biting her after treatment becomes infected?
choices: It prevents infected red cells from adhering to capillary endothelium
It kills sporozoites before they reach her liver
It eradicates dormant hypnozoites in her hepatocytes
It reduces gametocyte carriage in her blood
It blocks the Duffy antigen that merozoites use to enter red cells

explain.html:
The malaria life cycle has distinct stages in two hosts. The female Anopheles mosquito injects sporozoites, which go to the liver and become schizonts; in P. vivax and P. ovale some stay dormant as hypnozoites. Merozoites released from the liver infect red cells and cycle through ring, mature trophozoite and schizont stages, and some differentiate into gametocytes, the stage ingested by the mosquito when it feeds. Artemisinin-based compounds are the most active antimalarials: they act on the blood stage, clear early ring forms, and reduce gametocyte carriage.

Her smear shows the falciparum pattern: several rings in one cell, rings in red cells of every age, appliqué forms, and crescent gametocytes. Ghana is chloroquine resistant and she has uncomplicated disease, so oral artemether-lumefantrine is indicated. Because a mosquito can only be infected by taking up gametocytes, the drug property that limits onward spread is the drop in gametocytes. Her earlier fever was a separate infection, since falciparum has no liver stage that relapses.
explain.table:
Life-cycle stageWhere it isRole
SporozoiteInjected by the mosquito, travels to the liverStarts human infection
HypnozoiteDormant in hepatocytes (vivax, ovale only)Relapse months later; needs primaquine or tafenoquine
Ring and mature trophozoite, schizontRed cellsFever, hemolysis; target of chloroquine and artemisinins
GametocyteRed cellsIngested by the mosquito; reduced by artemisinins
why: Cytoadherence of infected cells to endothelium explains cerebral malaria, not infection of mosquitoes.
Sporozoites are injected by the mosquito into a person, so killing them protects the person, not the next mosquito.
Falciparum has no hypnozoite stage, so there is nothing dormant in the liver to eradicate.
The Duffy blood group antigen is the red-cell receptor for P. vivax, not a drug action and not a transmission step.
explain.takeaway: Anopheles mosquitoes are infected by ingesting gametocytes; artemisinin-based therapy acts on the blood stage and reduces gametocyte carriage, and falciparum has no hypnozoites.
explain.topic: Malaria transmission: gametocytes and artemisinin action
